analysis.one_liner: Makes agencies offset the cost of every major new regulation by repealing others.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the 116th Congress, dying after referral to two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a federal 'regulatory budget.' Every agency would have to identify at least two existing rules to repeal in order to issue any major new rule costing $100 million or more, and the White House budget office would cap how much total regulatory cost each agency may add each year, with a default of zero. It would also create task forces in every agency to review every existing regulation for repeal. The effect would be to make new federal protections on health, safety, wages, the environment, and finance far harder to issue.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that bear the cost of complying with federal rules — large manufacturers, energy and chemical producers, financial firms, and other regulated industries — would gain lower compliance costs and a structural brake on future rules. Supporters also argue small businesses and consumers benefit when compliance costs are passed on in prices.

how_it_helps.text: Every agency would have to establish a regulatory reform task force to review each existing regulation, estimate the cost savings of repealing or modifying it, and identify rules that are outdated, impose costs exceeding benefits, or eliminate jobs [S2][S3].

Agencies could not issue a significant regulatory action — generally one with a $100 million or larger annual economic effect — unless they identified at least two deregulatory actions to offset its cost, or the OMB Director approved it in writing in advance [S2][S3].

OMB would set an annual regulatory budget for each agency specifying the net allowable increase in regulatory costs, and if the Director set no amount, the default allowance would be zero new regulatory cost [S3].

The bill includes transparency requirements: task force membership, reports, and public comments would have to be posted online, and agencies would have to publish agendas of planned regulatory and deregulatory actions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules for clean air and water, workplace safety, food and drug safety, consumer and financial protections, and wage and labor standards would bear the cost: those rules would be far harder to issue or replace, and existing ones would be under standing review for repeal. The public would trade regulatory protections for lower compliance costs, and the benefits of regulation — prevented harm — would not be counted in the budget.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines costs as 'opportunity cost to society' and its offset and budget requirements count only the cost of regulation, not the benefits — lives saved, illness avoided, fraud prevented — so the arithmetic structurally favors repeal even when a rule's benefits far exceed its costs [S3].

The 'two-for-one' offset requirement would make it extremely difficult for any administration to respond to new problems — a new financial product, a new pollutant, a new workplace hazard — because every major new protection would require gutting existing ones [S2][S3].

Supporters acknowledge hidden costs: compliance spending is real, is spread across businesses and consumers, and is not tracked the way spending is, which is the problem the regulatory budget is meant to address [S3].

Critics of regulatory-budget proposals generally note that costs are highly uncertain and easy to overstate, so a zero-default budget could freeze needed rules on arbitrary cost estimates; this objection was not resolved in the bill text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has genuinely attractive features — public posting of task force work, published agendas, and a serious attempt to force agencies to account for costs they normally leave off the books. But its core mechanism counts only costs and never benefits, and its two-for-one and zero-default provisions would sharply restrict the government's ability to issue any major new protection, whatever its merits. The burden of the trade falls mostly on people who benefit from rules rather than on the firms that pay to comply with them, and the bill offers no process for judging whether an individual repeal would help or hurt the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Meadows introduced the bill on January 15, 2019, and it was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Reform and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On February 25, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law; that was the last action taken on the bill for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
Twenty-two House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regulated industries that would have faced the two-for-one offset and the annual regulatory cost cap are better off that the bill died, as is anyone who wanted existing federal health, safety, and financial rules left in place and new ones issuable. The public's existing rulemaking rules remain unchanged.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy and chemical producers, financial firms, and other companies facing federal compliance costs)
industries.note: The bill would give these industries a structural brake on new rules — every $100 million-plus rule would require repealing two others, and agency regulatory cost allowances would default to zero — while standing task forces reviewed existing protections for repeal. Their gain in lower compliance costs comes largely at the expense of the protections ordinary people get from those rules [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Office of Management and Budget / the executive branch
industries.note: The bill would hand the OMB Director sweeping power: setting each agency's regulatory cost allowance, approving major rules in writing, issuing waivers, and defining what counts as deregulation. That power could be used to block rules under any administration, concentrating gatekeeping authority in one political office [S3].

industries.industry: Federal regulatory agencies and the public programs they enforce (health, safety, environmental, labor, and consumer protections)
industries.note: Agency task forces would be required to review every regulation for potential repeal, and performance plans would grade officials on implementing deregulation, reshaping agency incentives away from issuing protections [S3].
